newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK HORSERACING CHIEFS EAGER TO STAMP OUT GRAFT.
newsitem.headline: HK HORSERACING CHIEFS EAGER TO STAMP OUT GRAFT.

text.p: Hong Kong's thriving racing industry has pledged to keep up the pressure in its bid to stamp out corruption.
The Jockey Club, which has dropped its "Royal" prefix, is also keen to keep attracting top riders and trainers from abroad after the handover of the British colony to China on June 30.
The sport was hit recently by one of its biggest scandals with police storming the Sha Tin racecourse, hauling 36 people away for questioning and charging five for illegal bookmaking.

Club chief executive Lawrence Wong promised to keep a wary eye open: "Our job is to make sure we protect the integrity and interests of the general public and make sure the playing field is level. The club is very determined to do that."

Hong Kong racing, which last weekend staged its last meeting before the handover, boasts a turnover expected to top US$12 billion for the year, a figure that puts the club among the top 150 companies on the Fortune 500 list.

The club has adopted an international stance with a series of races attracting jockeys and horses from Asia, Europe and North America. Hong Kong race meetings are broadcast via satellite to eight countries around the world.

South African Basil Marcus was this year's top jockey. Ivan Allan, who hails from Singapore, battled for top training honours with Frenchman Patrick Biancone and Australians John Moore and David Hayes.
Wong is eager that Hong Kong should continue to attract top talent from around the globe.
"In racing there is always going to be reliance on some of the critical mass of the foreign expatriates," Wong said.
"I think for the foreseeable future, we will always have the expatriate jockeys," he told Radio Hong Kong in an end-of-season interview on Wednesday.

The latest addition to the international jockey ranks will be top American Craig Perret, granted a licence to ride in Hong Kong for three months next season. The 1990 Kentucky Derby was among his 4,000 winners.
The season ended last Sunday with a world record bonanza when Hong Kong was seized by gambling frenzy.

The HK$S719 million prize money for the hugely popular Triple Trio wager smashed the last world horse-racing payout record of $US1.627 million in California in 1987, according to the "Guinness Book of Records."
The Jockey Club, a non-profit organisation which has a betting monopoly in Hong Kong, claims to rank among the world's five largest philanthrophic organisations.
Over the past decade, it has donated US$1.2 billion, transforming the face of Hong Kong with funds for schools, hospitals and sports facilities.
And racing authorities have pledged post-handover to keep up the flow of charity funds to Hong Kong, whose Chinese gamblers bet with such a passion.
